source: indian-defense.json :: Chapter 6: The Grünfeld Defense (promoted to its own opening)
intro: WELCOME. This is a realistic-opponent repertoire for Black's Indian Defenses — every reply to 1.d4 that meets 2.c4 with ...Nf6 instead of ...d5, sidestepping the Queen's Gambit complex entirely and fighting for the center with pieces instead of pawns (the "hypermodern" approach). Built the same way as the companion Sicilian and Queen's Gambit encyclopedias: main theoretical moves, common tries you'll actually meet, sharp lines, quiet positional systems, traps, and typical mistakes, every line verified move-by-move for legality. PLANNED TABLE OF CONTENTS — Chapter 1: Understanding the Indian Defenses (foundations — structures, breaks, plans). Chapter 2: The Nimzo-Indian Defense. Chapter 3: The Queen's Indian Defense. Chapter 4: The Bogo-Indian Defense. Chapter 5: The King's Indian Defense. Chapter 6: The Grünfeld Defense. Chapter 7: The Modern Benoni. Chapter 8: The Budapest Gambit and Other Rare Black Tries. Chapter 9: Traps and Tactics Compendium. Chapters will be built and appended one at a time, with every line verified for legality and spot-checked against current theory before being added.

tree.commentAfter: THE NEO-GRÜNFELD — fianchettoing before committing the queenside knight, a subtly different move order from the main Fianchetto Variation (Study 6.5) that avoids giving Black the option of transposing into King's Indian structures as easily.

AN IMPORTANT POINT — rather than e4 (which would transpose toward the main Exchange Variation, Study 6.1), White keeps the center flexible, since the knight hasn't committed to c3 and can't easily be met with ...Nxc3.

and White finally builds the center too, now that development is complete — this move order avoids some of the sharpest main-line Exchange Variation theory while reaching a structurally similar position, a popular practical choice for players who want the positional benefits without memorizing the deepest forced lines.
